ZAMA ZAMAS | CLOSER TO HOME

By: Chuma Kave | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Zama-Zamas have taken over a part of Benoni and communities want them out and some have learned to live with them

Unique Selling Point:
A full illegal operation in full view of the public.

Summary:
Communities in Benoni especially those living not far from Golden Drive are living in fear. Zama-Zamas are digging way closer to their doorstep and fearing the worst. They believe what happened in West Rand could be approaching the neighborhood soon. The intervention of the police has been slow to non-existence and the CPF is nowhere to be found. They are digging right outside the office parks and the business is losing tenants daily as workers live in fear. “You can’t even open a window…because they are just 10m away”. Right across the freeway, is the residential area where the Zama-Zama sometimes walk around brazenly. 

The Golden Drive is next to the suburbs like Morehill, Rynfield, Vlakfoentein, Kleinfontein

The business community put money together money and built a wall that it hopes will safeguard them from the Zama-Zamas entering their properties. There are regular explosions and shootings where the bodies are wrapped up in blankets and left next to the freeway. 
The Zama-Zama have also established their own informal settlement right behind the business premises where over 200 people live and work. The informal settlement is a hype of activity with multiple processing stations and a large trading market. Different stalls sell food, clothing, and alcohol and bakkies sell water. The traders are people from the township. Apparently, within the village, there’s also prostitution that takes place with girls that come from the township. 
The community feels like it is on its own and no one wants to do something…but…another group of community members and activists have found the Zama-Zamas to be extremely useful in keeping the township safe and have called for a humanitarian approach in dealing with them. Due to the fact that no one wants to do something, they have instead decided to engage the Zamas and found ways of using them as security in the area. “If you don’t bother them, they won’t bother you…”. They say the area used to suffer a lot from petty crime from criminals and since they engaged to look after the area, the crime has gone down drastically. 
It seems the area has two groups. Those who want them out immediately and those who have learned to live with them.



Case Study:
Lornette Joseph
H Hassan
Lionel Marks

Expert:
David Msiza

Hidden Camera: Yes
Reason for hidden camera: What exactly is happening inside that informal settlement where the miners live and operate?
It seems it won't be possible to enter the village with cameras as they are suspicious of everyone who looks like a stranger.

Script:


Zama zamas - Closer to Home #6397

OPENING: INTRO SEQUENCE: VIZ: Opening Scene: Visuals of Zamas throwing soil and water in the basin and working with their hands.
Music / Viz: zama searching for gold in the water / Viz: Move to Zamas working closer to the wall

1. Illegal mining is on the move… closing in on once quiet neighbourhoods… bringing danger… anxiety… fear.

Upsound Marinda: These residents are so scared. They don’t sleep at night.

2. As the Zama Zamas expand their operations… besieged residents cry for help.

Upsound Resident: They have increased in numbers. We feel threatened. We feel scared.

3. Abandoned, they’re left to fend for themselves… doing what they can to protect their homes… their lives.

Upsound zama: These communities are surrounded by gold….even if I go and dig in my yard, I’ll find gold.

VIZ SEGUE: DIP to Black


Link Govan: Blasting.. running gun battles.. informal structures mushrooming right on their doorstep. For these Benoni residents… daily life is becoming a nightmare. And they blame informal.. illegal miners.

Upsound Marinda: The mine dump next to the highway was a landmark of Benoni. It wasn't operable anymore and everything was fine. … Well, lately, you are so scared to go out outside of your home.

4. Marinda Beukes moved to Benoni, on Johannesburg’s East Rand, twenty years ago. Even then, the area’s once lucrative gold mines were already winding down.

PAUSE

Few had planned on how best to keep their defunct shafts sealed and fenced off in the long term.
PAUSE
But there’s still enough gold underground for illegal artisanal miners - or zama zamas - to scrape a living.

PAUSE
It’s a job done by hand, with rudimentary tools and explosives.

PAUSE
And as the zamas and their rock blasting crept ever closer, Marinda and her fellow residents set up an association as a first line of defence.

Upsound Marinda: We're trying to teach people to care for everybody and care for your own. So we started taking back our area. It's our area. We pay the taxes here.

Govan: What about blasting?

Upsound Marinda: Anything between 12 and 4:00 at night…The windows rattle. Your house rattles…Our animals are distraught and the people are awake immediately.

5: The influx of Zama zamas has seen an increase in crime, as they source the tools of their trade from the neighbourhood - like the rubbish bins they use for storage.

Visuals: CCTV Videos of people stealing the wheelie bins

Upsound Marinda:...Lately, the more security you put up on your property, the more they steal because they work underground. They use our security lights, our solar lights that we put on the security beams. They steal that gate motors. This last month has been gate motors because they can use all of that stuff in the mine. That's what they do. They steal what is needed that aren't just random things.

6: Marinda patrols the streets in her electric wheelchair, reporting anything suspicious to the residents’ online group.



7: The zama zamas work day and night, so the group is constantly on alert. Even so, they were powerless to stop the digging that disrupted these local businesses.

Viz: Zama by the wall

8: The zamas simply cut the fence and started digging. In response, the businesses have already spent about half a million rand putting up a wall.
PAUSE FOR VIZ - Viz: Govan inspecting the holes. Viz: The wall

But, just days after our visit, the wall was damaged as zamas went on a raid to steal lights.

Viz: zama shot peeping through the wall / Viz: Damaged wall / Pic: Incident reprot

Some of the miners are willing to talk. A mix of locals and foreigners, they’re working above ground, washing the soil and panning for gold. They insist they keep to their side of the wall.

Upsound Govan : They put the wall up

Upsound Zama: Sizephenza ngapa, thina engekhe singene ngapha (We only work this side, we can never enter that side)

Link Govan: Behind is where the illegal miners work and this road lead to the informal settlement where they live and conduct their trade. We’ve been warned not to go there.

9: Close to the nearby suburb, an entire village is flourishing. Entry is tightly controlled.

Viz: Drone shot of the village

10: It’s a world that exists above ground and below: a complex of temporary shelters and other structures surrounding the entrances to a maze of tunnels.

Viz: zama village
Viz: Govan driving to the gate

Link in the car: We’re on the road leading to the village for illegal miners. This is where their operations are based. This is where they refine the gold. This is where they have a market. We will try to go inside and we’ve been warned that its dangerous
Viz: Govan driving to the gate

11: At the entrance, we’re warned not to go any further.

Upsound security: …You see camera. No. My people are going to be fighting…camera
Govan: Can’t you arrange for us to go inside?
Upsound: hi, no, there’s gonna be trouble…those people here are not alright. They have illegal things
Govan: So they have guns? So if we go there we can get shot?


12: Our safety not guaranteed, we proceed while filming under cover…and encounter a chaotic but surprisingly organised community.

PAUSE

Some work underground…others process and trade gold in the village.

PAUSE

And a makeshift market appears to be thriving.

PAUSE FOR MUSIC …


13: Our time here is limited because we have a looming interview in the suburb. But, a message says she’s had a change of heart because of pressure from other residents.

VN1 - How can you be scared of the retaliation of illegal miners


14: We visit her and she tells us our presence here is causing anxiety in an already troubled community.

Upsound resident: What a battle! what a battle! I tell you, The pressure of the community is high. They are not wanting me to do it.
Govan: Why does the community not want you to talk?

Upsound resident: The zama zamas will know that we’re behind them and they are going to start taking over:

Govan : Do you feel sad about how today has gone in this whole situation?

Upsound Resident: i am. I feel that the community is crying wolf…They are not standing in what they believe. And yet on other days, you crying out and reaching out and saying, please, we need help.


15: We leave without real answers… but a sense of how the zamas are holding this suburb to ransom.

Viz: Govan interacting with locals on New Modda

16: We encounter more miners just outside her house.

Govan: People say they are scared of zama zamas
Upsound Zama: It’s the world on their own there.
if you don’t look for a problem, the problem won’t come to you.

Visuals: Inside the village

17: It’s clear from our undercover visit to the zama’s village that it’s attracting children, too. It’s why some residents, like this member of the local Community Policing Forum, want the situation dealt with humanely.

Upsound: You have a lot of…kids that are working in these areas. Some that go down are 14 and 15 years old. We cannot go out and shoot at them. We cannot go and harass them.

18: Since the community and zamas appear destined to co-exist, a way forward, he says, needs to be found together.

Upsound: We have some Zamas around us….they provide us sometimes with the Intel of what is going on around us. Whenever we need to know what’s happening, I consult with them…


Upsound News clips: Newzroom Afrika / eNCA

19: But, in this chaotic, lawless environment, it’s impossible to have a handle on everything. And in another dusty corner of the East Rand, that point was about to be made tragically clear.


Govan Link: As we were filming in Benoni, tragedy struck here in Boksburg, just 20 min away. Something similar is happening here - which shows that unregulated mining is dangerous and deadly.

20: A gas bottle - to be used as a primitive gold refining machine - has been cut open in one of these shacks. The fumes have killed 17 people.

Viz: the scene inside

21: These tools and buckets of soil are tell-tale signs of a full-scale zama operation - right where people live.

Viz: Police piecing equipments and taking them out.
Viz: Gavin walking around and more activities

22: Gauteng police commissioner General Elias Mawela is on the scene.

Upsound Mawela: …Illegal mining. It is a problem…that is why we find our hands full….

Upsound Govan: Do you think the police can stop illegal mining on the East End?

General Mawela: Not police alone, I repeat, not police alone. It will never be stopped by the police alone. It's a whole of government approac

Viz: New Modda at sunset

23: Back in Benoni, the sun is setting. The Residents’ Association sets out on patrol…and at a taxi rank dedicated to the illegal mining operation, the zama day shift makes way for night.

END: Reflective Link Govan: I’ve been covering illegal mining on the East Rand for over a decade. This is the worst I’ve ever seen it. What’s more frightening is that right now it looks like the community is in the space where there’s no clear path away from illegal mining. Zama-Zama’s have themselves part of this community and I worry that they are part of the future of the East Rand.


PROMOS
Promo 1
VO: Street cameras, fencing, patrols…raising their walls. How one community in Benoni is protecting itself from the illegal miners on their doorstep.
Upsound Steven: The local SAPS cannot fight this problem.
Upsound Marinda: We started taking back our area. It's our area. We pay the taxes here.


Promo 2
VO: Shootouts.. regular blasting.. this Benoni community is under siege - as zama zamas vow they will dig and continue digging .. even into suburbia.
Upsound Marinda: …They are going to invade us more and more and more…blasting with dynamite in a residential area is against the law, but there is no law.


Promo 3
VO: In one Benoni community, Zama-Zamas are digging ever closer to private properties … spreading fear throughout the area … but who is standing up to take back ther security?
Residents: They have increased in numbers. We feel scared.
Upsound Steven: The local SAPS cannot fight this problem. It”s impossible.
